title: The MongoDB Data Model
subtitle: BSON types, ObjectIds, and document structure
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: JSON is a great human-readable format, but it lacks precise data types. The number 42 and the string '42' look similar, dates become strings, and binary data can't be represented. This causes bugs, inconsistencies, and slow queries.
whyItExists.solution: MongoDB uses BSON (Binary JSON), which extends JSON with additional types: Date, ObjectId, Decimal128, Binary, Regular Expression, and more. BSON also encodes length prefixes so the engine can skip fields without parsing the whole document.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Understanding BSON types is essential when working with dates (use Date, not strings), monetary values (use Decimal128, not Double), unique IDs (use ObjectId), and binary data (use Binary instead of base64 strings).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: You rarely choose BSON types manually — MongoDB drivers automatically convert JavaScript/Python/Java types to BSON. The main decisions are around ObjectId vs custom _id and Double vs Decimal128 for precise decimals.

explainModes.beginner: BSON is like JSON but smarter. It knows the difference between a number and a date, so you don't have to store dates as strings like '2026-01-01'. MongoDB automatically converts JavaScript Date objects to BSON Date when you insert them.
explainModes.simple: BSON extends JSON with typed values: Date (not strings), ObjectId (auto-generated IDs), Binary (for files), and Decimal128 (for precise money amounts). MongoDB drivers handle the conversion automatically.
explainModes.standard: BSON is MongoDB's internal binary format for documents. It adds type information to JSON's typeless values, enables fast seek (via size prefixes), and supports types that JSON can't represent like Date, Binary, and ObjectId. Each document field has an explicit BSON type tag.
explainModes.technical: BSON is a little-endian binary format. Each element starts with a 1-byte type identifier, followed by a c-string key, then type-specific value bytes. The ObjectId is a 12-byte value: 4-byte Unix timestamp + 5-byte random value + 3-byte incrementing counter — this gives both approximate insertion order and global uniqueness across machines.
explainModes.deepDive: BSON type tags map to MongoDB's internal C++ types. The ObjectId's timestamp component makes it roughly sortable by insertion time, which is why sorting by _id gives approximate chronological order without an explicit createdAt field. Decimal128 (IEEE 754-2008) gives 34 significant decimal digits — critical for financial calculations where Double's IEEE 754 floating-point can introduce rounding errors (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3).

content.text: MongoDB stores documents as BSON (Binary JSON), an extension of JSON that adds type information and binary encoding. BSON supports all JSON types plus several additional ones that are essential for a database: Date, ObjectId, Binary, Decimal128, and more.

You write documents in regular JSON (or JavaScript objects), and the MongoDB driver automatically converts them to BSON before sending to the server. When reading, BSON is decoded back to native types in your language.

content.code:
// BSON types used in a real document
const user = {
  _id: new ObjectId(),              // ObjectId — 12-byte unique ID
  name: "Alice Sharma",             // String
  age: 30,                          // Int32 (or Double in some drivers)
  score: 95.7,                      // Double (64-bit float)
  balance: Decimal128("1234.56"),   // Decimal128 — precise money values
  active: true,                     // Boolean
  tags: ["admin", "editor"],        // Array
  address: {                        // Embedded document (nested object)
    city: "Delhi",
    zip: "110001"
  },
  createdAt: new Date(),            // Date (stored as 64-bit UTC ms since epoch)
  updatedAt: null,                  // Null
  avatar: Binary(Buffer.alloc(10)), // Binary — for files, images
  pattern: /^[a-z]+$/i,            // Regular expression
};

// Check the BSON type of a value
console.log(user._id instanceof ObjectId);  // true
console.log(user._id.toString());           // "507f1f77bcf86cd799439011"

content.definition: A 12-byte unique identifier automatically generated for the _id field of each document. Contains a 4-byte timestamp, 5-byte random value, and 3-byte counter. Because of the timestamp component, ObjectIds are roughly sortable by creation time.

content.text: Every MongoDB document must have a unique _id field. If you don't provide one, MongoDB automatically generates an ObjectId. The _id field is always indexed — queries by _id are instantaneous.
Always let MongoDB generate _id using ObjectId unless you have a natural unique key (like email or username). ObjectIds are globally unique across machines and contain a creation timestamp for free.
One of the most common mistakes in MongoDB is storing dates as strings instead of BSON Date objects. Always use new Date() so you can sort, compare, and query date ranges correctly.
Never store dates as strings like '2026-06-15'. Date comparison and range queries won't work correctly. Use new Date() or ISODate() in mongosh to store proper BSON Date values.

questions.question: What BSON type is used for the _id field by default?
questions.explanation: MongoDB uses ObjectId as the default _id type — a 12-byte value containing a timestamp, random component, and counter.

questions.question: What is the correct BSON type to use for storing a date?
questions.explanation: Always use BSON Date (new Date() in JavaScript) for dates. String dates cannot be sorted chronologically, and range queries won't work as expected.

questions.question: What additional information is encoded inside a MongoDB ObjectId?
questions.explanation: An ObjectId contains a 4-byte Unix timestamp, so you can extract the approximate document creation time with id.getTimestamp().

faq.a: Yes. Set _id to any unique value: a string email, an integer, or any value you choose. Just ensure uniqueness — MongoDB will reject duplicate _id inserts with an E11000 duplicate key error.

faq.q: What is the difference between Double and Decimal128?
faq.a: Double is a 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point, which is fast but can have rounding errors (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004). Decimal128 is an arbitrary-precision decimal type that is accurate to 34 significant digits — use it for monetary values to avoid rounding bugs.

faq.q: What is BSON and why doesn't MongoDB just use JSON?
faq.a: JSON is text-based and typeless — it cannot distinguish a date from a string, or store binary data. BSON is a binary format that adds explicit type tags and length prefixes to each field, making it faster to parse and encode, and supporting types that JSON doesn't have.

usedIn: Audit trails with creation timestamps from ObjectId
examples: Using email as _id for user collections to avoid duplicate accounts without an extra unique index
Extracting creation date from ObjectId to avoid storing a separate createdAt field
Using Decimal128 for product prices in e-commerce to avoid floating-point rounding issues
